## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Takkalajātaka* (Ja 446) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional framing narrative, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at Jetavana regarding a dutiful layman who supported his father [SuttaCentral]. 

In the verse narrative preserved in the commentary, a young boy confronts his father as the latter begins digging a square pit in the midst of a cemetery in the forest, asking why he is digging a hole when there are no edible bulbs (*takkalā*), tubers (*ālupāni*), or roots to be found (*na takkaḷā santi na ālupāni...*) [Fausböll 1887]. The aṭṭhakathā explains *takkalā* as a type of bulbous root (*piṇḍālukanda*) [Fausböll 1887]. At the conclusion of the story's teaching of the truths, the devoted son who maintained his father attains the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and the Buddha identifies himself as having been the wise boy (*paṇḍitakumāra*) in that past life [Fausböll 1887].

SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus shows extensive textual sharing between the Jātaka verses and the fourth volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* across 15 matches [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects cross-language alignments with passages in the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D0001) and the Chinese *Ekottarika-āgama* (T 125) [DharmaNexus].
